strengths: The paper is well-motivated and clearly written, asking a clean research question (can off-the-shelf MLLMs serve as retrievers without training?) and providing a coherent three-part answer.

The empirical evaluation is broad and convincing: 8 model families/scales on MMEB (36 datasets) and the MMEB-V2 video subset, with training-free results (e.g., 73.3 avg with Qwen2.5-VL-32B) that match or exceed supervised baselines trained on millions of pairs.

The probing experiments on 'lexicalization pressure' (Fig. 2, Fig. 7) are a genuinely interesting analysis, showing the final MLP sharply increases alignment with the LM head while decreasing semantic (synonym-pair) similarity, and the effect is replicated across 3B/7B/32B scales and other architectures (Table 5).

The 'framing effect' study on reranking label choices (Yes/No vs True/False vs MCQ) is a novel and useful diagnostic for MLLM-based rerankers, with careful methodology (label-order swapping, multiple prompt paraphrases) described in Appendix A.4.
Thorough ablations (Table 3) that isolate the contribution of each component, plus a reproducibility statement with runnable code in the supplement.
Honest limitations discussion (Appendix A.5-A.6) covering computational overhead and dependence on base-model capability.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty per component: skipping the last layer for embeddings, prompt engineering with semantic priors, and MCQ-style scoring are each simple and partly known techniques (e.g., calibration/prompt-format sensitivity is documented, e.g., Zhao et al. 2021, which the authors themselves cite); the contribution is primarily their combination and analysis rather than a new method.

Cost and latency of the reranking stage are not quantified in the main results. It is unclear whether Table 1/2 numbers include reranking, and MLLM-based reranking over k candidates can be very expensive; Figure 5 varies k but no wall-clock/throughput numbers are given, making the claimed practicality hard to assess.

Some baselines in Table 1 use much smaller backbones (e.g., Phi-3.5-V-4B, LLaVA-OV-7B) while the headline FreeRet result uses a 32B model; the claim of 'outperforming models trained on millions of pairs' partly conflates backbone capacity with method quality, although the 7B comparison to GME-7B is fair.

The 'theoretical analysis' (Lemma 1) is a simplified and somewhat informal gradient argument whose assumptions (e.g., final MLP converges to a projection onto span(W)) are not rigorously established; it adds intuition but little formal support.

The semantic-retention probe relies on cosine similarity of hidden states for 250 synonym pairs, a narrow proxy; broader semantic metrics or downstream correlation would strengthen the causal claim that lexicalization pressure causes retrieval degradation.
The framing-effect analysis is restricted to one dataset (ImageNet-1K subset of MMEB) and a handful of label pairs; generality of the claimed phenomenon across tasks remains underexplored.
Claims about arbitrary modality combinations (Fig. 6) rest on qualitative case studies with Qwen2.5-Omni rather than quantitative evaluation on audio/omni retrieval benchmarks.

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation: the paper spans 36 MMEB datasets plus the MMEB-V2 video subset, seven MLLM backbones across three model families and three scales (Table 1), with ablations that isolate each of the three proposed components (Table 3), which is a reasonably thorough experimental setup.

The probing analysis of 'lexicalization pressure' (Fig. 2, Fig. 7, Table 5) is a nice piece of analysis: measuring cosine similarity between consecutive layers and alignment with LM-head columns across three Qwen2.5-VL scales and additional architectures (Llava-OV, InternVL) gives the main embedding modification (bypassing the final MLP) an empirical motivation rather than being a blind trick.

The identification of label-framing sensitivity in LLM reranking (Fig. 4, Table 3c) is a practically useful observation, and the appendix honestly describes the mitigation protocol (prompt paraphrasing, label-order swapping).

Useful systems-level discussions: the omni-modal retrieval demonstration (Fig. 6), the candidate-pool scaling analysis (Fig. 5), and the LVBench experiment (Table 4) show the framework's versatility beyond the standard MMEB setting.
The paper includes a reproducibility statement with runnable code and an explicit limitations section (A.6) that acknowledges computational overhead and dependence on backbone quality.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty of the individual components. Each contribution is an inference-time heuristic: removing the final MLP layer, adding prompt constraints ('capture the semantics of...', 'do not use function words'), and converting Yes/No reranking into a multiple-choice question. The framing-effect finding is essentially a restatement of known calibration/context bias effects (the paper itself cites Zhao et al. 2021), and the proposed MCQ remedy is a straightforward application of that prior work to retrieval. The combined system is useful, but the methodological delta over E5-V-style prompting is thin for a main-track paper.

The 'lexicalization pressure' theory (Lemma 1, Corollary A.0.1) is weak. The gradient argument shows the cross-entropy gradient lies in the span of vocabulary embeddings, but the leap to 'the final MLP layer learns h' ≈ P_W(h)' is asserted, not proven, and no experiment directly tests this projection claim. The theory section adds little beyond decoration.

Potential benchmark contamination is not addressed. A central claim is that training-free retrieval 'outperforms models trained on millions of pairs' (Abstract, Fig. 1c), but MMEB tasks (ImageNet-1K classification, N24News, etc.) very likely appear in the pretraining corpora of large MLLMs such as Qwen2.5-VL-32B. Without any contamination analysis, the headline comparison of a 32B training-free model against 7B fine-tuned baselines is confounded — part of the advantage may reflect memorization rather than a genuine 'training-free paradigm' advantage.

Unfair backbone asymmetry in headline comparisons. The best FreeRet results (73.3 average) come from Qwen2.5-VL-32B, while the strongest supervised baselines use 7B backbones. There is no supervised baseline built on a comparable-scale backbone, so claims that FreeRet 'surpasses existing supervised results' conflate scale effects with the training-free argument. A fine-tuned Qwen2.5-VL-32B (even with LoRA) control is missing.

Computational cost is acknowledged but never quantified. Reranking with an MLLM over k candidates multiplies inference cost substantially; Fig. 5 shows accuracy vs. candidate count but no latency/FLOPs measurements, and the scalability discussion (A.5) offers only generic suggestions (lighter models, pre-filtering) without any experiments. For a paper claiming practical deployability of unified retrieval+reranking, the absence of efficiency numbers is a significant gap.

Main results lack variance reporting or significance testing (only the small probing study in Fig. 2b reports std), so improvements of 1-2 points in Table 1 (e.g., 70.7 vs 70.7 for UniME) are hard to interpret. The prose even notes 'FreeRet-7B competes head-to-head' when the numbers are essentially tied.

Some claims are overstated relative to evidence: 'closing a critical gap in their role as generalists' and 'state-of-the-art competitive' rest on a single benchmark family (MMEB/MMEB-V2), and the generic 'framing effect' generalization is drawn from one model family on one dataset subset with three prompt paraphrases (A.4).

Presentation issues: Fig. 1c plots the 'training-free' points at an unlabeled x-axis position that visually overstates the efficiency comparison; the abstract and introduction repeat the same three contributions nearly verbatim, suggesting insufficient distillation.

strengths: Well-motivated question: whether off-the-shelf MLLMs can serve as retrieval engines without any post-training, addressing a real scalability limitation of contrastive post-training approaches.

The paper is not just a system; it includes genuine analysis: the 'lexicalization pressure' probing experiments (Fig. 2, Fig. 7) elegantly locate where the final MLP distorts representations toward token prediction, and the appendix generalizes this across 3B/7B/32B scales and three model families (Qwen, InternVL, LLaVA) with consistent gains (Table 5).

The 'LLM framing effect' observation (semantically equivalent Yes/No vs True/False label pairs yielding divergent reranking accuracy) is a novel and interesting empirical finding, with a reasonable mitigation via MCQ reformulation and a context-free logit analysis for label bias.

Comprehensive evaluation: 36 MMEB datasets plus MMEB-V2 video tasks, across 9 backbone models of varying scales and families, with per-component ablations (Table 3) showing each of the three contributions contributes measurably.

Strong empirical outcomes: consistently and substantially outperforms the training-free E5-V baseline and surpasses models trained on millions of pairs (e.g., MMRet-7B trained on 26.2M pairs), and is competitive with MMEB-supervised SOTA at 32B scale.

Useful discussion of broader implications (omni-modal retrieval without pairwise data, unified retrieval+reranking+generation in one model, LV-Bench gains), an explicit reproducibility statement with code in the supplement, and an honest limitations section covering inference overhead and dependence on base-model capability.
weaknesses: The technical contributions are individually simple (skip the last MLP, add prompt constraints, reframe binary judgment as MCQ). The novelty rests mainly on the analysis, and prior text-LLM work (PromptEOL, context-free calibration of Zhao et al. 2021) already covers much of the underlying ground; the paper's positioning as three 'advances' somewhat oversells known techniques.

Risk of prompt overfitting to the evaluation benchmark: the 'task alignment' priors and MCQ template are task-specific and appear designed with knowledge of MMEB's task taxonomy. This slightly undercuts the 'training-free generality' claim; a held-out evaluation where prompts were fixed before seeing the benchmark is not provided.

Several claims rest on thin or anecdotal evidence: the semantic-loss/vocabulary-noise argument (Fig. 3) is illustrated with a single cherry-picked qualitative example; the 'framing effect' benchmark analysis uses only the ImageNet-1K subset of MMEB; and Lemma 1 / Corollary A.0.1 is an informal sketch (gradient orthogonality does not by itself establish that trained MLP outputs collapse onto span(W)).

Computational cost is under-analyzed relative to its practical importance. Reranking is the dominant expense, yet the main results do not report latency, number of candidates reranked in the headline tables, or FLOPs, making comparisons to embedding-only baselines (e.g., GME, VLM2Vec) potentially unfair. The efficiency discussion is deferred to qualitative suggestions in Appendix A.5.

The 32B headline result that 'surpasses supervised results' involves a substantially larger model than most baselines; the size-matched comparison (7B) is competitive but not superior to UniME, and the paper's Figure 1c messaging could be clearer about this model-size asymmetry.
No statistical significance testing or variance reporting for the main benchmark results, despite averaging over 36 datasets where per-dataset variance could be reported.

strengths: Well-motivated question with a clear diagnosis: the paper provides probing experiments (Fig. 2, Fig. 7, Fig. 8) showing that the final MLP layer exerts 'lexicalization pressure' that degrades semantic structure, and connects this to a concrete, actionable fix (bypassing the final MLP). The cross-lingual synonym/antonym analysis in Appendix A is a nice piece of evidence supporting the mechanism.

Extensive empirical support: evaluation on MMEB (36 datasets), MMEB-V2 video subsets, Flickr30K/COCO, six MLLM backbones spanning three families and multiple scales (Tab. 6), plus cross-lingual evaluation. The ablations (Tab. 3) cleanly isolate each component's contribution, and the layer-choice ablation is validated beyond Qwen (Tab. 5).
The framing-effect study for reranking (Fig. 4, Tab. 3c) is an interesting and practically relevant observation, with the MCQ reformulation yielding consistent gains across models.

Honest treatment of costs and limitations: Tab. 9-10 report latency and memory, Appendix F discusses scalability to 100M+ candidates, Appendix I explicitly states limitations, and failure modes are analyzed (Fig. 9). A demo package is provided, aiding reproducibility.

Practical significance: a plug-and-play recipe that preserves the generative/omni-modal abilities of the underlying MLLM and unifies embedding, reranking, and generation is useful, as demonstrated by the LVBench long-video results (Tab. 4) and omni-modal examples (Fig. 6).
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: each component is individually simple and largely known—skipping final layers echoes prior analyses of task-specific vs. semantic layers (Zeiler & Fergus; PromptEOL/MetaEOL line), prompt-based steering is standard prompt engineering, and MCQ-style calibration of binary judgments closely follows Zhao et al. (2021). The originality rests mainly on the empirical synthesis and analysis rather than new techniques.

The headline 'beats models trained on millions of pairs' depends heavily on the expensive reranking stage: FreeRet-embed (53.7) trails GME (56.0) and UniME-V2 (69.6), while FreeRet-50 (70.7) requires scoring up to 50 candidates per query per model. While Tab. 9-10 quantify this, the abstract/introduction framing slightly overstates the embedding-stage contribution.

Prompt sensitivity is underexplored. The three lightweight constraints (task alignment, semantic grounding, noise suppression) are presented as principled, but the paper does not report how brittle results are to paraphrasing these prompts, nor how many prompt variants were tried during development—raising mild overfitting-to-benchmark concerns for a method claiming benchmark-agnostic generality.

Some analysis is suggestive rather than conclusive: the framing-effect probing uses a single dataset (ImageNet-IK subset) with three paraphrases; the theoretical Lemma C.1 is a simplified linear model that does not strictly apply to trained nonlinear MLPs; and the claim that deeper-layer removal hurts because 'deeper layers capture essential semantic abstractions' is a hypothesis without direct verification.

Baselines for the reranking comparison are somewhat favorable to the authors: several supervised rows in Tab. 1 are embedding-only models, and the reproduced E5-V number (39.8) is notably lower than other reported values in the literature; clarification of evaluation protocols (candidate pools, Precision@1 computation) would strengthen confidence.
Cross-lingual evaluation (Tab. 7) relies on LLM-translated versions of MMEB, which introduces translation noise acknowledged by the authors but limits the strength of that generalization claim.

strengths: The core question—whether off-the-shelf MLLMs can serve as retrievers without any training—is well motivated and timely, and the training-free embedding result is genuinely improved: FreeRet-embed (53.7 avg on MMEB) substantially outperforms the reproduced training-free E5-V baseline (39.8) with zero training data.

The probing analysis of 'lexicalization pressure' (Fig. 2, Fig. 8, Tab. 3a) is a nice diagnostic contribution: the observation that the final MLP drives representational collapse (α dropping below 0.3, synonym/antonym/random similarities converging) is supported across model scales (3B/7B/32B) and architectures (Qwen, InternVL, LLaVA, Tab. 5), and the resulting fix is simple and effective (+5–6 points).

Evaluation breadth is above average for this line of work: MMEB, video tasks on MMEB-V2, cross-lingual (ZH/FR) evaluation, Flickr30K/COCO, LVBench integration, computational efficiency analysis (Tab. 9-10), error analysis (Fig. 9), and honest limitations (Appendix I) acknowledging latency overhead and dependence on base-model capability.

The model-agnostic deployment across ~10 backbone variants (Tab. 6) and omni-modal retrieval demonstration (Fig. 6) support the plug-and-play generality claim, and a code demo is provided for reproducibility.
weaknesses: The headline claims are inflated by an unfair comparison protocol. The central claim that FreeRet 'outperforms models trained on millions of pairs' and 'matches MMEB-supervised methods' rests entirely on FreeRet-r50 (reranking top-50 candidates per query) being compared against baselines that rerank top-5 or top-10 (e.g., UniME-V2 r5 at 69.6, MM-Embed r10 at 54.9). Reranking 50 candidates with a 7B MLLM multiplies inference cost ~5-10x; under a matched r5/r10 budget (Tab. 10), FreeRet achieves 60.4-67.8, which does not clearly exceed trained baselines. The embedding-only result (53.7) remains well below supervised methods (69-70). The abstract and introduction present the r50 number as the method's headline performance without adequately flagging the budget asymmetry.

Limited novelty of the three components. Bypassing the final layer for embeddings is a well-known layer-choice heuristic in the embedding literature; the controlled prompt constraints are standard prompt engineering; and the 'LLM framing effect' is a direct rediscovery of the calibration/surface-form competition biases of Zhao et al. (2021), which the paper itself cites. Casting binary relevance as MCQ is an incremental prompt change, and the MCQ-vs-binary comparison (Fig. 4) is only demonstrated on the ImageNet-1K subset rather than the full benchmark suite.

The theoretical appendix (Lemma C.1) is superficial: it linearizes the MLP, derives the standard cross-entropy gradient, and concludes that training aligns hidden states with the LM head span. This does not actually establish that the final MLP causes 'lexicalization pressure' in the nonlinear trained network, nor that discarding it preserves semantics—it is post-hoc rationalization of an empirical observation, presented with more formality than it merits.

Several evidential and presentation issues undermine confidence: Tab. 8 lists 'FreeRet_r20' twice with different numbers (apparent duplication/typo, one presumably meant to be a different setting); the claim that FreeRet 'preserves generative abilities' (abstract, §4.4) is never empirically validated with any evaluation of the underlying MLLM's QA/reasoning performance after retrieval use; typos appear in core method descriptions ('reqired', 'concent', Fig. 3 template).

The prompt constraints ('You are required to assess if <placeholder> is related to <placeholder>') encode task priors that must be tailored per task, which softens the 'arbitrary modality combination with zero adaptation' narrative—§3.4 concedes 'MCQ content may be adjusted to suit the needs of each task', and the paper does not measure sensitivity to these prompt choices.

The framing-effect analysis on model scale (§4.3) offers a conjecture about why 7B is more sensitive than 3B ('larger models capture finer semantic distinctions') that is speculative and untested; the causal link between context-free logit asymmetry and downstream accuracy is asserted from correlation on a single task.

strengths: The paper asks a well-motivated question — whether off-the-shelf MLLMs can serve as competitive retrievers without any post-hoc training — and answers it convincingly with a simple, plug-and-play framework.

The analysis is unusually thorough for a 'simple trick' paper: probing experiments localize lexicalization pressure to the final MLP layer (Figs. 2, 7, 8), ablations isolate each component (Tab. 3), and the effect generalizes across model families and scales (Tab. 6), supporting the mechanism claim rather than just reporting gains.

The identification of the 'LLM framing effect' in reranking (equivalent binary labels yielding divergent accuracy) is an interesting and practically useful observation, and the MCQ mitigation is well supported by Tab. 3c and Fig. 4.

Empirical results are strong: FreeRet-2B outperforms GME-7B trained on 8M pairs, and FreeRet-7B (70.7) matches or exceeds supervised MMEB-trained systems (UniME-V2 69.6), with additional validation on MMEB-V2, Flickr30K/COCO, cross-lingual splits, and long-video retrieval (LV-Bench).

Reproducibility and self-criticism are handled well: a code demo is provided, efficiency/latency/memory is measured (Tab. 9-10), failure modes are analyzed (Fig. 9), and limitations are honestly stated rather than hidden.
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate. Bypassing the final layers of a generative model to obtain embeddings, and using choice-based prompts/logit scoring, echo well-known findings in the text-embedding literature (PromptEOL, MetaEOL, Echo-Embedding, intermediate-layer representations). The paper acknowledges these lines but does not sharply delineate what is new beyond porting them to the multimodal setting.

There is a potential evaluation-hygiene concern: the three prompt constraints (task alignment, semantic grounding, noise suppression) and the choice of MCQ framing appear to have been selected/tuned on MMEB itself, which is also the headline benchmark. No held-out prompt-validation split is described, so the 'training-free' claim is partially undercut by implicit prompt engineering on the test suite; the cross-lingual and Flickr/COCO results partially mitigate this but do not resolve it.

The theoretical appendix (Lemma C.1 / Corollary C.2) is essentially a restatement that cross-entropy gradients live in the span of the embedding matrix; it is trivially true and adds little analytical insight beyond the empirical probing.

Practical cost of the reranking stage is significant: at n=50 candidates, latency grows to ~2.97s (7B) versus 0.47s embedding-only, and the best reported results rely on this large reranking pool. The scalability discussion in Appendix F remains qualitative.

Some methodological details are underspecified for exact reproduction (embedding normalization, how hidden states are pooled for multi-token/multimodal inputs, candidate selection criterion), and the variance/significance of the reported Precision@1 gaps (e.g., 70.7 vs 69.6) is not assessed.
The framing-effect claims rest on a small set of label pairs and one task subset (ImageNet-IK with 3 rephrasings); broader evidence across tasks would strengthen the generality of this finding.
